pathways.title: African American research
pathways.summary: Start with yourself and work back through standard records (vital, census) and collateral lines; 1870 is the first census naming all free people. When standard records run out, move to specialized sources: Freedmen's Bureau and Freedman's Bank records, USCT/pension files, slavery-era records of enslavers, and state-specific collections.
cautions: Records are sparse before 1870; enslaved people typically appear unnamed or only in records of enslavers (probate, tax, deeds).
FamilySearch notes only about 15% of formerly enslaved people used a former slaveholder's surname, and many changed surnames 1865-1875 — do not infer descent or slaveholder from surname alone.
About 10% of the African American population was free before the Civil War (per FamilySearch) — check free people of color records too.
Freedmen's Bureau and Freedman's Bank are separate organizations with separate NARA record groups.
Historical records contain offensive terminology; present with content warnings.

steps.title: Begin with yourself and oral history
steps.detail: Document living memory and recent vital records generation by generation, using census to reconstruct family groups and researching collateral relatives.

steps.title: Exhaust standard state and county records first
steps.detail: Use the same record types as any U.S. research (state/county wiki pages) back toward 1870 before turning to specialized sources.

steps.title: Read a specialized how-to guide
steps.detail: LOC recommends beginners read a guide to African American research; it lists selective titles and notes the pre-1870 challenge.

steps.title: Search Freedmen's Bureau records (1865-1872)
steps.detail: Field office records (labor contracts, marriage records, relief rolls, complaints) are name-rich; digital images are on FamilySearch, organized by microfilm publication.

steps.title: Use federal records on Black soldiers and families
steps.detail: NARA's African American Heritage hub points to Black Family Research (post-Civil War agencies), pension files, and related publications.

steps.title: Move to state-specific slavery and bondage collections
steps.detail: Return to the FamilySearch state African American pages for records not commonly used elsewhere (e.g., slavery and bondage collections).

sources.title: LOC: African American Genealogical Research – How to Begin
LOC: African American Family Histories and Genealogies

pathways.title: Indigenous / Native American research (U.S., with Canada note)
pathways.summary: Use standard genealogy methods to prove or disprove a family tradition of Native ancestry, building the tree relationship by relationship until a reliable record identifies an ancestor as Native. Identify the tribe (or the tribes associated with the ancestor's locality), then search federal records (BIA agencies, Indian census rolls 1885-1940s, allotment, Dawes for the Five Tribes) and tribal records. In Canada, Library and Archives Canada holds Indian Status records (RG 10) and Indian Registers.
cautions: Tribal enrollment is determined by each tribe, not the BIA or genealogists; requirements vary by tribe. The app must not imply that a record establishes eligibility.
The BIA has no database of enrolled members and does not do genealogy research.
Many family traditions of Native ancestry are unproven; LOC frames research as proving or disproving them. Do not infer ancestry from surnames, appearance, or DNA ethnicity estimates.
NARA: records under 75 years old (incl. student records) may be restricted under FOIA (b)(6).
Many tribal offices require enrollment before allowing access to members' records (FamilySearch).
Canada: many LAC documents are restricted; 'Status' is a legal category under the Indian Act and eligibility rules changed over time (e.g., Bill C-31). Historical terminology may be offensive.

steps.title: Start with yourself and home sources
steps.detail: Gather family papers, vital records, and oral history; work backward generation by generation to reach a documented lineal ancestor.

steps.title: Treat Native ancestry as a hypothesis to test
steps.detail: Use genealogical methods to prove or disprove a family tradition, building relationships event by event.

steps.title: Identify the tribe or the tribes of the locality
steps.detail: If the tribe is unknown, study tribes associated with where the ancestor lived and the nearest reservation/BIA agency.

steps.title: Search federal records by time and place
steps.detail: Use NARA's American Indian and Alaska Native records (agency records, special censuses, school and allotment records); many are only on paper/microfilm.

steps.title: For Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole: use Dawes records
steps.detail: Final Dawes Rolls, census cards (searchable by name in NARA Catalog), and enrollment application jackets.

steps.title: Contact the tribal government about enrollment
steps.detail: Enrollment criteria are set by each tribe; apply directly to that tribe with documentation of direct lineal descent.

pathways.title: Adoption research
pathways.summary: Adoption records are governed by state law and are often sealed. Start by learning the specific state's access rules (nonidentifying vs identifying information, original birth certificates, mutual consent registries, intermediaries). For older (pre-1900s) adoptions, look in county court probate/guardianship records, orphan train and institution records, maternity home records, and church baptismal records.
cautions: Adoption records are frequently sealed; access to identifying information generally requires consent of the person whose information is disclosed, and rules differ by state.
Distinguish nonidentifying information (health, heritage, physical description) from identifying information (names, addresses).
Mutual consent registries release identifying information only when both parties register and consent.
The CWIG state statutes summary is marked 'Current Through: 12-31-2019' — verify current state law before relying on it.
Searches and reunions can be emotionally difficult; CWIG frames search as affecting both adoptees and birth families. The app should avoid auto-surfacing living relatives' identities.
Catholic sacramental records are not public records; access is governed by diocesan policy.

steps.title: Learn your state's access law
steps.detail: Use Child Welfare Information Gateway state-by-state summaries to see who can obtain nonidentifying and identifying information and original birth certificates.

steps.title: Request nonidentifying information and register with a mutual consent registry
steps.detail: States such as New York operate adoption information registries that release identifying data only on matched consent.

steps.title: Read the search guidance factsheet
steps.detail: CWIG's Searching for Birth Relatives factsheet covers the search process, information access, and support resources for adoptees and birth families.

steps.title: For early adoptions, search county court probate/guardianship records
steps.detail: Contact the clerk of the court in the county of adoption for probate and guardianship records.

steps.title: Check institutional sources: orphan trains, foundling homes, maternity homes, church records
steps.detail: Children's Aid Society and NY Foundling Hospital sometimes hold birth-parent records; Catholic baptismal records may help.

sources.title: Child Welfare Information Gateway: Access to Adoption Records
CWIG: Access to Adoption Records – New York

pathways.title: Displacement: Holocaust-era, WWII displaced persons, refugees
pathways.summary: There is no single list of Nazi-persecution victims and survivors; research means following trails. Identify the pre-war hometown first, search the Arolsen Archives online archive (camp, forced labor, DP records), then USHMM's survivor/victim name database and free research services; use the Arolsen inquiry form or USHMM to request deeper searches. Follow DP emigration into U.S. immigration records.
cautions: Records are incomplete: the ITS/Arolsen archive lacks names of many murdered on arrival or who died on death marches, and is thinner for Eastern Europe and most ghettos.
USHMM's survivor Registry is not online, to protect survivors' and families' privacy.
Living survivors and descendants are involved — handle personal data carefully.
Documents use German abbreviations and period terms; use the Arolsen e-Guide/USHMM glossary.
Claims for indemnification are handled by other bodies (Arolsen points to Claims Conference).

steps.title: Identify the town the person lived in before the war
steps.detail: USHMM notes the town is often the most useful entry point for choosing archives.

steps.title: Search the Arolsen online archive
steps.detail: Search names across camp, forced-labor and DP documents; use the e-Guide to interpret documents.

steps.title: Search USHMM's Holocaust Survivors and Victims database
steps.detail: Millions of personal records; about 80% online, full database onsite.

steps.title: Request free research help
steps.detail: USHMM staff search the ITS Digital Archive free for survivors and families of victims.

steps.title: Submit an Arolsen inquiry
steps.detail: If online search fails, use Arolsen's inquiry form, supplying as much detail as possible.

steps.title: Trace post-war emigration
steps.detail: Follow DPs into U.S. arrival and naturalization records (see migration pathway; USCIS A-Files for post-1944 immigrants).

sources.title: USHMM: How Can I Learn What Happened to Individuals During the Holocaust?
USHMM: International Tracing Service Digital Archive
USHMM: Resources on Survivors and Victims

pathways.title: Migration and immigration (passenger lists, naturalization)
pathways.summary: Work out roughly when and where the immigrant arrived and naturalized. Federal passenger arrival lists run ~1820-1982 (by port); before 1820 use published compilations. Naturalization before Sept 27, 1906 could occur in any court of record, so check local courts; after 1906 federal courts dominate and USCIS holds duplicate C-Files. USCIS Genealogy Program (fee-based) provides A-Files, AR-2s, C-Files, Registry and Visa files for deceased immigrants.
cautions: Arrival records are restricted for 75 years (FOIA needed); records older than 75 years are public.
Immigrants were not renamed on arrival; search original-language spellings (e.g., Giuseppe for Joseph).
NARA generally lacks pre-1906 state/local court naturalizations and usually lacks the naturalization certificate itself.
USCIS Genealogy Program covers deceased immigrants only and charges fees (see its fee schedule).
Ellis Island Foundation database records may contain historical language with inaccurate cultural/geographic references.
Castle Garden (castlegarden.org) did not respond during verification — treat as unavailable.

steps.title: Gather arrival clues before searching
steps.detail: Collect names, approximate arrival and birth years, port, and travel companions.

steps.title: Search passenger arrival lists by port and date
steps.detail: NARA holds lists ~1820-1982 by port; many older than 75 years are digitized by partners (FamilySearch free; Ancestry/Fold3 subscription).

steps.title: Search the Ellis Island Foundation Arrival Records
steps.detail: Covers Ellis Island/New York and other ports; use ethnic spellings.

steps.title: Locate naturalization by date and court
steps.detail: Pre-1906: any court of record; post-1906: federal courts; two-step process (declaration then petition).

steps.title: Request USCIS Genealogy files
steps.detail: Order an index search, then a record request for A-Files, AR-2, C-Files, Registry or Visa files.

steps.title: Use FamilySearch's U.S. emigration/immigration guide
steps.detail: Background, online record lists, and state-by-state immigration pages.
